title: impermanence
hook: impermanence; the leaf, the mood, the year

segments.voice: Yesterday: the bell, a sound you follow down to silence. Your line was arrive. Did some ordinary sound become your bell? Day eleven.

Look at a leaf in October. Last spring it was a tight green bud. In summer it was so ordinary nobody noticed it. Now it's red and gold and loose on the branch, and next week it'll be on the sidewalk. Now set this morning's mood beside this one. Look at last year: a worry that kept someone up in March can be hard to even recall by fall. The leaf, the mood, the year. They're all doing the same thing, at different speeds. They're passing. The Buddha asked people to look at that, closely, until they saw it.

Anicca. In Pali, nicca means permanent, lasting, constant. Put an a in front and you get the opposite: not lasting. Impermanence. It's the first of what Buddhists call the three marks of existence, the three things true of everything that's made of parts and conditions. Anicca, impermanence. Dukkha, which you already know. And anatta, which is tomorrow. The Dhammapada, in Max Müller's translation, puts the first one in four words: "All created things perish." Now, that sounds obvious. Everyone knows things change. But here's the catch. It's easy to know it the way we know the sun is a star: true, and no help at all on a Tuesday. A good mood gets held as if it'll stay. A bad week feels like forever. An ending still startles. So the Buddha didn't teach anicca as a fact to agree with. He taught it as something to see, again and again, in small things, until it sinks in. Watch a breath: it comes, and goes. Watch a thought: it arrives, and leaves. Watch a sound, like yesterday's bell, fade away. And there's another side to it. Impermanence isn't only sad news. It's what makes change possible at all. If things were permanent, your grief would never soften. Your bad habit would never break. The seed would never grow. The same fact that takes the leaf in October brings the bud in April. This passes, both ways.
screen: `ANICCA — NOT LASTING.` · `THE FIRST OF THREE MARKS.` · `ALL CREATED THINGS PERISH.` · `WHY GRIEF CAN SOFTEN.` · then, large: `THIS PASSES.`

segments.voice: The bell will give you about forty-five seconds. Watch something pass. Start with the breath: notice that each one begins, and ends, and is never quite the same as the last. Then notice sounds around you, arriving and leaving. If a feeling comes up, watch that too. You're not trying to hold anything or push anything away. Just watching things come and go, like leaves. The bell holds the time.
Anicca. Impermanence, the first of the three marks. Everything made of parts is passing, the hard things and the good ones. Eleventh word.
Your line: this passes. Today, when a strong feeling comes, good or bad, say it inside: this passes. Then watch to see if it's true. Day eleven.

howItsDone: Buddhists reflect on anicca in meditation by watching breath, sensations and thoughts arise and pass, and in daily life by recalling that all conditioned things change; some traditions use images like falling leaves, candles and sand mandalas swept away after completion.

match.prompt: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.

myth: it's also why grief can soften, habits can break, and seeds can grow.
anicca is the first of the three marks of existence

fork.setup: you're having the best evening in months. friends, food, a warm night. you notice it will end. what does the teaching on anicca suggest?
options: hold on tight so it lasts.
stop enjoying it. it's ending anyway.
see it clearly, passing, and be fully in it while it's here.
fork.reveal: anicca isn't a reason to stop enjoying. seeing that the evening is passing can make you more present to it, and less crushed when it ends.

original.note: Pali: impermanent. a (not) + nicca (permanent). Sanskrit: anitya.

trapdoor: what you thought: everything changes. obviously.
what it means: a fact easy to agree with and hard to live by, practiced until it's seen in every breath, mood and year.
what a scholar hears: anicca, the first of the tilakkhaṇa, the three marks. Dhammapada 277 pairs it with dukkha and anatta in verses 278 and 279.

notes: Editor review 2026-10-01: hook no longer tells the listener what their mood and worries did, and drops the overclaim 'changes everything'; 'we're startled every single time' and 'everyone knows and nobody lives by' softened; cut 'the part that's easy to miss'.
Dhammapada 277 in Max Müller begins with the quoted phrase in quotation marks: 'All created things perish,' he who knows and sees this... Confirm exact wording.
Dhammapada 277–279: three verses on impermanence, suffering and not-self. Confirm the numbering.
'Three marks of existence' (tilakkhana): confirm naming for this path.
Voice said Müller puts it 'in five words'; the quoted phrase is four words, corrected to 'four words'.
